content: Sodium periodate refers to two distinct chemical compounds, both of which are sodium salts of the periodate ion. These compounds are: 1. Sodium metaperiodate (NaIO4), commonly abbreviated as m-periodate. 2. Sodium orthoperiodate (Na5IO6), commonly abbreviated as o-periodate. Both of these salts are valuable in synthetic chemistry due to the oxidative properties of the periodate ion. Sodium periodate has a density of 3,865 kg/m³ and is soluble in water. Upon heating, it undergoes decomposition to produce sodium iodate (NaIO3) and oxygen gas. This decomposition reaction is catalyzed by manganese(IV) oxide. It is important to note that the correct pronunciation of periodate is per-iodate, not period-ate. Uses of Sodium Periodate 1. Oxidation of Cellulose: Sodium periodate is employed to oxidize cellulose, resulting in the formation of a biocompatible and biodegradable compound. This modified cellulose can be utilized in various biomedical applications, such as sutures, scaffolds for tissue engineering, or drug delivery systems. 2. Saccharide Ring Opening: In solution, sodium periodate can cleave saccharide rings at vicinal diols, producing two aldehyde groups. This reaction is frequently used to label saccharides with fluorescent molecules or other tags, such as biotin. 3. Selective Labeling of RNA: Since the reaction requires vicinal diols, periodate oxidation is often applied to selectively label RNA. This is because ribose, the sugar in RNA, contains vicinal diols, whereas deoxyribose, the sugar in DNA, does not.
